In the Brønsted–Lowry theory, a polyprotic acid, Zn(H O) 2 4 21( ) aq , donates hydro­ gen ions in succession to make all the product ions. The second product, Zn(OH)2, is amphoteric; it can react as ­either acid or base. It is only slightly soluble in pure water (its Ksp is only 1.9 3 10217). If enough acid is added to solid Zn(OH)2, the OH2 ligands are removed, forming the soluble Zn21 ion; if enough base is added, OH2 ligands attach to form the soluble Zn(OH)4

21 (zincate) ion. Thus, Zn(OH)2 is soluble in strongly acidic or strongly basic solutions but is only slightly soluble at intermediate pH values (Fig. 16.15). This amphoterism can be used to separate Zn21 from other cations that do not share the property. For example, Mg21 adds a maximum of two OH2 ions to form Mg(OH)2, a sparingly soluble hydroxide. Fur­ ther addition of OH2 does not lead to the formation of new complex ions. If a mixture of Mg21 and Zn21 ions is made sufficiently basic, the Mg21 precipitates as Mg(OH)2 but the zinc remains in solution as Zn(OH) , 4 22 allowing the two to be separated. 16.6 Selective P recipitation of I ons

One way to analyze a mixture of ions in solution is to separate the mixture into its components by exploiting the differences in the solubilities of compounds contain­ ing the ions. To separate silver ions from lead ions, for example, a search is made for compounds of these elements that (1) have a common anion and (2) have widely different solubilities. Lead chloride is far more soluble in water than is silver chloride. Consider a solu­ tion that is 0.10 m in both Ag1 and Pb21. Is it possible to add enough Cl2 to pre­ cipitate almost all the Ag1 ions but leave all the Pb21 ions in solution? If so, a quantitative separation of the two species can be achieved.
